newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ debt mkts continue to claw back ground at close.
newsitem.headline: NZ debt mkts continue to claw back ground at close.

text.p: Figures in brackets compare against previous day's close
FUTURES PHYSICAL YIELD
OVERNIGHT CASH 9.05 PCT (PREV 9.05) US 5-YR 5.97 (PREV 6.04)
* NZ debt rallies back across curve after Friday's selling
* All eyes on Winston Peters
* Traders roll over positions ahead of futures close out
New Zealand debt markets continued to claw back lost ground at Monday's close, thumbing a ride on the back of global markets' recovery from Friday's sharp sell-off.

Midday trade in Tokyo saw U.S. Treasury prices edge higher on short-covering activity after they changed tack on the back of a modest November non-farm payrolls report. Local sentiment was also helped by a short-covering rally in Australian bonds.

New Zealand yields dropped seven to eight points across the curve, with the money market also helped along by a jump in the currency's Trade-Weighted Index to 67.05, more than 50 points above Friday's closing level.
The 90-day bank bills ended 10 points stronger at 8.40 percent, while the front futures contract climbed eight to 91.63 with several traders rolling out positions ahead of Wednesday's close-out.

Dealers said despite the market's rally, few traders were prepared to take large positions with the market on tenterhooks ahead of an announcement from the nationalist New Zealand First Party on its preferred coalition partner.

NZ First, which holds the balance of power, has been negotiating with both the centre-left Labour Party and the caretaker conservative National Party in a bid to form a new government after October's general election.

The pace of coalition negotiations was stepped up dramatically over the weekend and NZ First leader Winston Peters said his party hopes to make a decision on Tuesday. Labour is holding lengthy talks with the left-wing Alliance to discuss the latter's support for a Labour-NZ First coalition on money supply and confidence issues.
Parliament is scheduled to reconvene on Thursday.

"I think most people have got that nervous sweat on board," one dealer said, adding that he expected a volatile knee-jerk market reaction to NZ First's decision, followed by more considered trading when the market saw what compromises had been
reached.
"Personally I think the market is expecting NZ First to go with someone -- I don't think they're expecting Peters to go and sit out on his lonesome," he said.
